newsitem.title: JAPAN: Foreigners line up to issue samurai bonds.
newsitem.headline: Foreigners line up to issue samurai bonds.

text.p: A boom in samurai bonds is heating up, with more overseas issuers lining up to sell the bonds to yield-hungry Japanese investors during the winter bonus season.
Many experts expect the trend to last, while others warn that investors may not be fully aware of risks involved in investing in dual-currency samurais.

"Investors are attracted by the high coupon and by the unique characteristic of dual samurais that the interest payment is in yen," said a senior analyst at a bank's research arm. "Those things are emphasised, but risks such as the danger of currency fluctuations are not publicised widely."
A samurai is a bond issued in Japan by a non-Japanese denominated in yen. A dual-currency samurai is issued in yen, with interest paid in yen and redeemed in other currencies.
Underwriters said the volume of dual-currency samurai bond issues in November exceeded 300 billion yen ($2.63 billion) in a single month for the first time.
Issues of samurai bonds so far this year have totalled nearly 3.5 trillion yen ($30.7 billion), of which dual-currency samurais account for nearly 40 percent.

"The pace of samurai issuing hasn't gone down. The boom is continuing, particularly given the yen 's continuing weakness (against the dollar)," said Masaru Hamazaki, deputy manager at Yamaichi Research Institute.
The appetite of the investors' buying of foreign bonds has increased significantly since the yen fell from 79.75 to the dollar in April 1995 to its current level of about 114 yen.
Record-low interest rates on domestic savings accounts have also prompted Japanese investors to buy the samurais, which offer attractive yields.
In addition, private investors will have extra cash this month as Japanese companies pay their semi-annual bonuses.

Big names issuing dual-currency samurais recently include International Business Machines Corp and General Motors Corp, while underwriters say the governments of Thailand and Argentina are waiting to issue samurai bonds.
But some analysts said they cannot understand why the dual-currency samurai issues are so popular.

"Considering the foreign exchange fees the investors have to pay when converting (other currencies) into yen after redemption, the issues are not all that attractive," said the senior analyst at a bank's research arm.
Recent dual-currency samurai issues will be redeemed mainly in U.S. dollars, Australian dollars and New Zealand dollars.

In the Tokyo market, brokerages charge a foreign exchange fee of about 1 yen for each U.S. dollar an investor sells or buys, while the fee is 2 yen for an Australian dollar and about 4 yen for a New Zealand dollar.
Holders of the bonds may have to unload them at a big discount if they decide to sell them before maturity, analysts said, due to their low liquidity.
